headline: BULLISH
headline_tag: Price above a still-falling 200-day average; participation remains narrow

action.title: SCALE UP acquisition budget
action.detail: The market is in an early-stage uptrend with medium confidence (66/100). That supports a measured increase in acquisition spend, weighted toward active-trader and non-stablecoin channels, while holding some budget in reserve: fewer than half of recent days closed above the long-term average, that average is still declining, and long-term interest rates are high. This is a budget-posture view built on past data, not trading advice and not a forecast.

reasons: BTC is 17% above its 200-day average (Mayer Multiple 1.17).
90-day return of +35% with weekly RSI at a firm 60.
Only 48% of the last 90 days closed above the 200-day average.
200-day average still falling (-5% over 90 days); price 33% below all-time high.
watch: The main tension is between a strong headline gain (+35% over 90 days, Fear & Greed at 71) and a trend that has not fully confirmed: breadth is 48% and the 200-day average is still sloping down at -5% over 90 days. A 200-day slope turning positive and breadth moving well above 50% would strengthen the read; price falling back below the 200-day average would weaken it. The 5.26% 10-year yield, and markets being split on an October Fed rate rise ahead of the 27 October FOMC meeting, is the macro backdrop to monitor.
analysis: Short-term, Fear & Greed reads 71 (Greed), but actual positioning is more restrained than that label implies: the funding z-score of +0.92 shows leveraged longs paying a somewhat above-normal premium without being stretched, and the long/short ratio of 1.38 is only a modest long tilt. Open interest is about $7.7B, DVOL is 35.5 and the VIX is 15.9, so both crypto options and equity markets are pricing calm rather than stress; realised volatility sits at the 50th percentile of its two-year range and Bollinger width is 18%, neither compressed nor expanded. The stablecoin supply ratio of 5.4 means sidelined stablecoin liquidity relative to BTC market cap is moderate. The derivatives picture is consistent with that: PANews, citing CoinGlass, reported on 29 September that total crypto liquidations over the prior 24 hours were about $325M, fairly evenly split between longs ($194M) and shorts ($131M), which is a two-sided shake-out rather than a one-directional flush. On the macro side, Rio Times reported on 30 September that bitcoin settled at US$83,622 (+0.14%) on Tuesday after weak US job-openings and consumer-confidence data cut market-implied odds of an October Fed rate rise to about 51.5% from 70.9%. Put together, sentiment is optimistic while leverage and volatility are ordinary, so the greed reading is not yet backed by crowded positioning.

Medium-term, weekly RSI of 59.8 is firm but well short of overbought, and the 90-day rate of change of +35% marks a strong recovery leg. The quality of that gain is thinner than the headline suggests: only 47.8% of the last 90 days closed above the 200-day average, so the advance rests on a relatively recent move rather than a long, consistent run of strength. The 50-day average sits 8.4% above the 200-day (golden-cross side), which supports the trend even as breadth lags behind it. Active addresses are 5% above their yearly average, a mild pickup in network use, and BTC dominance of 58.3% shows activity concentrated in bitcoin rather than rotating broadly into altcoins. Flows are supportive without being dramatic: the pipeline's latest daily spot ETF net flow is about +$66M, and Rio Times, citing SoSoValue data, reported roughly US$31M of net inflow on Monday 28 September, an eighth straight session of net inflows. The next scheduled FOMC meeting is 27 October 2026, and the same report notes markets are currently split roughly evenly on a rate rise at that meeting, which makes it the main scheduled macro date inside this window.

Long-term, price is 17% above its 200-day average (Mayer Multiple 1.17), yet that average is still falling (-5.1% over 90 days). In other words, price has reclaimed the trend line before the trend line itself has turned up, which is an early-recovery configuration rather than a confirmed mature uptrend, and it is why the trend score (+0.23) is the weakest of the three. Valuation is unremarkable: the 200-week multiple of 1.26 is mid-range, price remains 33.2% below its all-time high, and the Puell Multiple of 1.28 shows miner revenue in a normal band; the Pi-Cycle gap of -55% is far from the zone that has historically accompanied cycle tops (both are context only, not scored). Macro is the clearest cross-current: the US 10-year yield is 5.26% against a fed funds rate of 3.63%, a wide gap that means long-dated government debt offers a meaningful competing return to risk assets, and Rio Times reported the 30-year at 5.57% on 30 September. Structural demand remains large, with cumulative spot ETF net inflows of about $57.7B and public companies holding roughly 1.28M BTC, a base of longer-horizon holders that did not exist in earlier cycles. All of these readings are trailing and describe conditions already in place, not forecasts.

team_notes.marketing: Lean into non-stablecoin and active-trader channels: the +35% 90-day move, Fear & Greed at 71 and an eight-session run of spot ETF net inflows (Rio Times, citing SoSoValue) give campaigns a credible recovery story. With breadth at only 48% and conviction at medium, lead with trend and product value rather than FOMO urgency, and avoid 'confirmed bull market' claims. Funding (z-score +0.92) shows leverage is not crowded, so keep stablecoin-first channels defended and some spend flexible while rate expectations around the 27 October FOMC meeting remain unsettled.
